The driver manual specifies 15–48 V DC as the rated driver range, while the SG-6010HB catalog lists 12–48 V for the actuator. Therefore a 12 V supply should not automatically be treated as a rated operating point for the driver-equipped system.

Final driver hardware revision, firmware, second encoder, connector set, current limits, brake function and any expansion interface still require order-level confirmation.

docs.title: Exoskeleton and Wearable-Robot Evaluation
docs.text:
The SigGear catalog explicitly identifies SG-6010HB as an exoskeleton joint motor.

For an exoskeleton or wearable robot project, evaluate at least:

  • Joint position: hip, knee, ankle, shoulder, elbow or auxiliary axis
  • Continuous assistance torque
  • Peak torque and allowed peak duration
  • Required output speed and range of motion
  • Maximum joint diameter, thickness and mass
  • Radial / axial / overturning load path
  • Backdrivability or holding behavior
  • Driver, encoder and communication architecture
  • Duty cycle, ambient temperature and heat path
  • Power-off safety strategy

Open the Exoskeleton Joint Selection Guide

docs.text:

  • Research robot joints
  • Low-profile actuator modules
  • Custom human-assist mechanisms

Suitability for any application must be confirmed from the actual torque-speed cycle, packaging, load direction and control requirements.

docs.title: SigGear Sales and Inquiry Knowledge
docs.text: This section provides a controlled public workflow for qualifying customer requirements, selecting a preliminary product candidate and preparing a safe response. It is intended for sales staff, distributors and AI-assisted inquiry handling.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text: Stage Purpose Guide 1. Qualify Collect the minimum information needed to understand the project Customer qualification checklist 2. Match Compare the requirement with canonical SigGear product pages Product matching workflow 3. Respond Answer the customer first, state boundaries and request missing information Inquiry response policy 4. Draft Use a controlled structure without inventing parameters or commercial terms Reply templates 5. Quote Confirm technical and commercial readiness before issuing a formal quotation Quotation readiness checklist

docs.title: Core Rule
docs.text:
A public product page supports preliminary selection. It does not by itself authorize a final technical commitment, price, delivery time, customization promise or production release.

Use the product model index, machine-readable product records and sales usage review matrix together.

docs.title: Public and Private Boundary
docs.text:
This public repository may contain generic inquiry questions, response structures and approved public product information.

Do not add:

  • Customer names, addresses, contact details, messages or drawings
  • Customer-specific requirements that could identify a project
  • Prices, discounts, internal MOQ rules, costs or margins
  • Private quotations, payment terms or negotiation strategy
  • Unreleased product data, restricted drawings or NDA material

Customer-specific work belongs in an approved private project or customer-management system.

docs.title: SigGear Customer Qualification Checklist
docs.text: Ask enough questions to identify a real application and avoid recommending a product from one attractive parameter alone. Start with the minimum questions and add detail according to the customer's technical level.

docs.title: Five Essential Questions
docs.text:
1. What type of robot or equipment are you developing?
  2. What continuous torque, peak torque and output speed do you need?
  3. Do you prefer an integrated actuator or a separate gearbox and motor?
  4. What are your estimated prototype quantity and annual quantity?
  5. What is the main problem with your current solution or supplier?

Suggested English wording:

What type of robot or equipment are you currently developing? What continuous torque, peak torque and output speed do you need? Do you prefer an integrated actuator or a separate gearbox and motor? What is your estimated prototype quantity and annual quantity? What is the main problem with your current solution or supplier?

docs.title: Engineering Requirements
docs.text:
Collect the following before final selection:

  • Application and exact axis or installation position
  • Concept, prototype, validation or mass-production stage
  • Continuous torque
  • Peak torque and peak duration
  • Rated and maximum output speed
  • Acceleration, deceleration and complete motion cycle
  • Operating voltage and available current
  • Maximum outer diameter, thickness, length and weight
  • Radial, axial and overturning loads
  • Backlash, accuracy and repeatability targets
  • Duty cycle, ambient temperature and cooling method
  • Noise, vibration and service-life targets
  • Required encoder, driver, brake and power-off behavior
  • CAN, RS485, EtherCAT or other communication requirement
  • Required control modes and protocol
  • CAD, drawing, datasheet or test-data requirement

For a robot with multiple joints, collect a separate requirement set for every axis.

docs.title: Project and Decision Information
docs.text:
• Company name, country and website
  • Current supplier or current drive architecture, when the customer is willing to share it
  • Main technical or commercial pain point
  • Expected supplier-selection date
  • Prototype deadline and production target
  • Technical decision maker and purchasing contact
  • Prototype quantity and estimated annual quantity
  • Delivery country or destination for freight evaluation
  • Preferred communication method

docs.title: Simplified Questions for a Non-Technical Contact
docs.text:
If the customer appears to be an owner, buyer or early-stage founder, begin with:

  1. What will the motor, gearbox or actuator be used for?
  2. What torque and speed do you need, if known?
  3. What is the maximum product size?
  4. What voltage will the equipment use?
  5. How many pieces do you need for the first order?
  6. Where should the order be delivered?
  7. What is the easiest way to contact you?

Do not send a long technical questionnaire before answering the customer's first question. Ask the smallest useful set, then continue after the customer responds.

docs.title: Qualification Outcome
docs.text:
Classify the inquiry as one of the following:

  • Standard candidate identified: published model is a reasonable starting point.
  • Engineering review required: customization or configuration confirmation is necessary.
  • Insufficient information: required torque, speed, size or architecture is missing.
  • No published match: the requirement is outside the current public product range.

docs.title: SigGear Inquiry Response Policy
docs.text: This policy defines the order, evidence and language used in customer replies.

docs.title: Response Order
docs.text:
1. Answer the customer's explicit question with confirmed information.
  2. State which product or family may be a preliminary candidate.
  3. Explain any configuration or evidence boundary.
  4. Ask for the smallest useful set of missing requirements.
  5. Request the preferred contact method when useful.
  6. State the next action, such as engineering review, model confirmation or quotation preparation.

Do not begin with a ten-minute company introduction or a long questionnaire.

docs.title: Short Company Introduction
docs.text:
Use only after the customer's application is understood:

We are SigGear, a Chinese manufacturer specializing in precision reducers and integrated robot joint actuators. Our joint modules can integrate the motor, reducer, encoder and driver, and we also support customized planetary and cycloidal solutions for robotic applications.

The wording “can integrate” is intentional. It does not mean that every model automatically includes a driver, encoder or every communication interface.

docs.title: Information Sources
docs.text:
Use information in this order:

  1. Canonical model page
  2. Matching product master-data record
  3. Sales usage and technical review status
  4. Application and selection guides
  5. Private engineering confirmation for the exact quoted configuration

If two sources conflict, stop and open a product-data review. Do not choose the more favorable value.

docs.title: Claim Rules
docs.text:
• Distinguish continuous torque from peak torque and request peak duration.
  • State whether the driver and encoder are included, optional or external.
  • Confirm CAN, RS485, EtherCAT, PID and control modes for the selected electronics and firmware.
  • Do not promise noise, life, efficiency, thermal or backdrivability values without applicable evidence and conditions.
  • Do not claim certification beyond the certificate holder, scope, model and standard.
  • Do not describe a product video as a controlled noise test.
  • Do not describe a preliminary candidate as a perfect match.

docs.title: Price, Lead Time and Customization
docs.text:
Do not invent or reuse a price, discount, MOQ, tooling fee or lead time from another project. Before a formal quotation, confirm:

  • Exact model and configuration
  • Prototype and production quantity
  • Customization scope
  • Required documents and testing
  • Delivery destination
  • Payment and shipping terms through the approved private process

For a custom request, state that feasibility, engineering cost and lead time are subject to technical review.

docs.title: Reply Style
docs.text:
• Use simple English for a buyer or company owner.
  • Use structured technical detail for an engineer.
  • Answer first, then list the information required from the customer.
  • Use bullets for parameters and questions.
  • State uncertainty directly and define how it will be confirmed.
  • Never expose another customer's project, price or drawing as evidence.

docs.title: SigGear Product Matching Workflow
docs.text: Use this workflow to create a preliminary shortlist. Do not describe a product as a perfect match until the complete requirement and ordered configuration have been reviewed.

docs.title: Step 1: Identify the Required Architecture
docs.text: Customer need Starting product family Motor, reducer, encoder and driver in one compact robot joint Robot joint actuators Compact high-torque joint using cycloidal transmission Cycloidal joint modules Separate precision reducer for integration with a motor Planetary gearboxes Miniature motor and gearbox assembly Micro gear motors Flat motor or short-axial joint drive Flat BLDC motors and joint drives Compact wheel or hub drive Hub gear motors

docs.title: Step 2: Screen Torque and Speed
docs.text:
Compare continuous torque with rated torque. Compare the customer's required peak torque together with peak duration, current limit, duty cycle and cooling.

Never use peak torque as the only selection value. A candidate must satisfy the complete torque-speed cycle.

docs.title: Step 3: Screen Mechanical Integration
docs.text:
Check:

  • Outer diameter, thickness, length and mass
  • Reduction ratio
  • Mounting interface and shaft
  • Radial, axial and overturning loads
  • Backlash, accuracy and repeatability
  • Shock, impact and structural conditions

External loads must be reviewed separately from output torque. Significant cantilevered or tendon loads may require additional bearing support.

docs.title: Step 4: Screen Electrical and Control Requirements
docs.text:
Confirm:

  • Operating voltage and current limits
  • Driver inclusion
  • Encoder or Hall-sensor configuration
  • Position, velocity and torque-control requirements
  • CAN, RS485, EtherCAT or other interface
  • Protocol, baud rate, command set and feedback data
  • Brake, holding and power-off behavior

An interface name alone does not confirm protocol compatibility.

docs.title: Step 5: Screen Environment and Validation Needs
docs.text: Check duty cycle, ambient temperature, cooling, ingress protection, noise, vibration, service life and required test evidence. Do not transfer a product-level IP rating to the complete customer machine.

docs.title: Step 6: Screen Project Readiness
docs.text: Confirm prototype quantity, annual forecast, project stage, selection date, required documents and delivery destination. These inputs affect configuration, engineering review, quotation and freight evaluation.

docs.title: Standard Candidate
docs.text: A canonical public model is a reasonable starting point and no unconfirmed modification is required. The quotation must still state the exact configuration.

docs.title: Configured Standard Product
docs.text: The mechanical model may be standard, but driver, encoder, cable, connector, communication or firmware must be selected and confirmed.

docs.title: Custom Engineering Project
docs.text: The customer requires a changed ratio, shaft, interface, housing, electronics or performance target. Engineering feasibility, development scope, cost and lead time require separate review.

docs.title: No Published Match
docs.text: State this clearly. Do not force-fit the closest model or invent an unreleased solution.

docs.title: Final Check
docs.text: Before recommending a model, read its canonical product page and the sales usage and review status. If the requirement conflicts with a prohibited shortcut, stop and request engineering review.

docs.title: SigGear Quotation Readiness Checklist
docs.text: Use this checklist before issuing a formal quotation or making a technical commitment.

docs.title: Customer and Project
docs.text:
• Company and country identified
  • Application and exact installation position understood
  • Project stage confirmed
  • Technical decision maker or responsible contact identified
  • Prototype schedule and supplier-selection date understood
  • Preferred contact method recorded privately

docs.title: Technical Requirement
docs.text:
• Continuous torque confirmed
  • Peak torque and peak duration confirmed
  • Rated and maximum speed confirmed
  • Voltage and current availability confirmed
  • Size and weight limits confirmed
  • Radial, axial and overturning loads reviewed
  • Duty cycle, temperature and cooling understood

docs.title: Product and Configuration
docs.text:
• Canonical model page reviewed
  • Product master-data record reviewed
  • Sales usage and prohibited shortcuts checked
  • Exact model, ratio and hardware configuration identified
  • Included and excluded components listed
  • Optional electronics, cables and connectors identified
  • Customer-specific modifications listed
  • Controlled drawing or internal technical source reconciled privately

docs.title: Commercial Inputs
docs.text:
• Prototype quantity confirmed
  • Estimated annual quantity confirmed
  • Customization scope confirmed
  • Required testing and documents confirmed
  • Delivery destination confirmed

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Correct datasheet or public product link selected

  • Test evidence matches the model and conditions
  • Certification claim matches the certificate scope
  • Quotation states configuration assumptions and exclusions

docs.title: Readiness Outcome
docs.text:
• Ready for formal quotation: technical configuration and commercial inputs are complete.
  • Preliminary quotation only: assumptions and unresolved items are stated clearly.
  • Engineering review required: technical feasibility or customization is unresolved.
  • Not ready: critical application, quantity or delivery information is missing.

docs.title: Quick Robot Joint Actuator Sizing Workflow
docs.text:
1. Define the joint position, payload, link geometry and complete motion cycle.
  2. Estimate gravity, acceleration and external-force torque.
  3. Separate continuous torque from peak torque and define peak duration.
  4. Check output speed, power, voltage and controller current limits at the same operating point.
  5. Confirm diameter, thickness, length, weight and external bearing loads.
  6. Compare planetary, cycloidal and integrated-actuator architectures.
  7. Confirm encoder, driver, communication, thermal and safety requirements.
  8. Validate the selected actuator in a representative prototype.

docs.title: Purpose of This Guide
docs.text:
A robot joint actuator should be selected from the complete axis requirement, not from one torque value or a product-family label. The joint position, payload, link geometry, acceleration, external forces, duty cycle, installation envelope, bearing loads, feedback architecture and controller limits all affect the final choice.

This guide provides a practical screening workflow for humanoid robots, quadruped robots, robotic arms, exoskeletons and other rotary-axis systems. Final model approval requires engineering review and prototype validation.

docs.title: Step 1: Define the Joint and Mechanism
docs.text:
Prepare a separate requirement sheet for each axis. A shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee or ankle normally has a different load case, motion profile and installation limit.

Record:

  • Joint or axis position
  • Payload and moving-link mass
  • Link lengths
  • Center-of-gravity locations
  • Joint angle range
  • External process forces
  • Mechanical stops and collision loads
  • Whether the axis is horizontal, vertical or gravity loaded
  • Customer-side bearings, belts, pulleys, gears or linkages

Do not apply one actuator specification to every axis of the robot.

docs.title: Step 2: Estimate Robot Joint Output Torque
Gravity Torque
docs.text:
For an initial one-axis estimate, gravity torque may be approximated by:

T_gravity = m × g × r × sin(theta)

where:

  • m is the supported mass
  • g is gravitational acceleration
  • r is the distance from the joint axis to the center of gravity
  • theta describes the mechanism orientation relative to gravity

The worst posture may not be the robot's normal operating posture, so review the full joint-angle range.

docs.title: Acceleration Torque
docs.text:
The torque required to accelerate the reflected inertia may be estimated by:

T_acceleration = J × alpha

where:

  • J is the total inertia reflected to the joint output
  • alpha is angular acceleration

Include the payload, links, tooling and any other moving components.

docs.title: External-Force Torque
docs.text:
An external force acting at a distance from the joint axis creates torque:

T_external = F × r

where F is the external force and r is the perpendicular lever arm.

docs.title: Preliminary Total
docs.text: A preliminary requirement should include gravity, acceleration, external forces, friction and mechanism losses. These equations are screening tools only. Flexible structures, impact, control behavior, load sharing and multi-axis dynamics may require a more complete model.

docs.title: Step 3: Separate Continuous and Peak Torque
docs.text: Continuous torque and peak torque are not interchangeable.

docs.title: Continuous Torque
docs.text: Continuous torque must cover sustained motion, repeated cycles and holding conditions without exceeding the approved thermal limits of the selected motor, gearbox and driver configuration.

docs.title: Peak Torque
docs.text:
Peak torque is used for short events such as acceleration, disturbance recovery, impact response or starting under load. Specify:

  • Required peak torque
  • Peak duration
  • Frequency of peak events
  • Time between peaks
  • Controller current limit
  • Battery or bus voltage
  • Cooling and ambient conditions

Never treat a published peak-torque value as a continuous rating.

docs.title: Step 4: Define Speed and the Complete Motion Cycle
docs.text:
Provide:

  • Rated output speed
  • Maximum output speed
  • Acceleration and deceleration
  • Travel angle
  • Cycle time
  • Holding time
  • Rest time
  • Direction-reversal frequency

Mechanical output power at an operating point is related to torque and angular speed:

P = T × omega

Torque and speed must be checked at the same operating point. A product's maximum torque and maximum speed may not be available simultaneously.

docs.title: Step 5: Establish the Installation Envelope
docs.text:
Define the maximum:

  • Outer diameter
  • Axial thickness
  • Total length
  • Weight
  • Cable and connector space
  • Driver-board space
  • Brake space
  • Mounting-flange envelope

Include the complete installed assembly, not only the reducer body. Bearings, output interfaces, covers, connectors and cable bend radius can consume significant space.

docs.title: Step 6: Review Radial, Axial and Overturning Loads
docs.text:
Output torque alone does not describe the structural load on a robot joint.

Provide:

  • Radial load
  • Axial load
  • Overturning moment
  • Load direction
  • Distance from the load to the output bearing
  • Impact or shock conditions
  • Customer-side bearing arrangement

The output bearing and housing must be evaluated together with the robot structure. An external bearing or additional support may be required when the joint has a large cantilevered load or overturning moment.

docs.title: Step 7: Define Positioning and Mechanical Behavior
docs.text:
Specify the completed-axis targets for:

  • Backlash
  • Positioning accuracy
  • Repeatability
  • Angular resolution
  • Stiffness or compliance
  • Backdrivability
  • Holding behavior
  • Direction-reversal response

Gearbox backlash is only one part of joint behavior. Encoder position, bearing clearance, housing stiffness, link compliance, assembly tolerances and controller tuning also affect the result.

docs.title: Step 8: Choose a Transmission and Product Architecture
docs.text: SigGear publishes both planetary joint actuators and cycloidal joint modules. Neither transmission type should be selected from a general rule alone.

docs.title: Planetary Joint Actuators
docs.text:
Planetary joint actuators may be evaluated when their published torque, speed, dimensions and configuration fit the application. SigGear's published planetary joint-actuator range includes SG-6010C, SG-6010D and SG-8021.

View planetary robot joint actuators

docs.title: Cycloidal Joint Modules
docs.text:
Cycloidal joint modules may be evaluated when the selected model's torque, speed, installation and configuration match the axis requirement. SigGear's published range includes CPM-100-25, CPM-80-25 and CPM-78-39.

View cycloidal joint modules

docs.title: Published Starting Points
docs.text:
Model Transmission Rated torque Peak torque Rated output speed Configuration note SG-6010C Planetary 6 Nm 18 Nm 310 rpm Driver and encoder functions depend on selected configuration SG-6010D Planetary 16 Nm 50 Nm 100 rpm Available with or without integrated driver SG-8021 Planetary 10 Nm 30 Nm 160 rpm Driver and encoder functions depend on selected configuration CPM-100-25 Cycloidal pinwheel 25 Nm 75 Nm 60 rpm Available with or without integrated driver CPM-80-25 Cycloidal pinwheel 10 Nm 50 Nm 120 rpm Available with or without integrated driver CPM-78-39 Cycloidal pinwheel 20 Nm 52 Nm 48 rpm Standard catalog configuration uses Hall sensors and has no integrated-driver claim

The table is a preliminary shortlist only. Dimensions, weight, external-load capacity, thermal behavior and control configuration must also be checked.

docs.title: Step 9: Define Encoder, Driver and Communication Requirements
docs.text:
Confirm whether the project requires:

  • Motor commutation feedback
  • Output absolute position
  • Incremental or absolute encoder
  • Position control
  • Velocity control
  • Torque or current control
  • CAN
  • RS485
  • EtherCAT or another project-specific interface
  • External controller or integrated driver
  • Required communication rate and protocol details

Driver, encoder, communication and closed-loop functions are model- and configuration-specific. Do not assume that every actuator includes the same electronics.

CPM-78-39 must be treated separately: its standard catalog configuration uses Hall sensors and does not support a general claim of an integrated driver or absolute encoder.

docs.title: Step 10: Review Voltage, Current and Power Architecture
docs.text:
Specify:

  • Nominal bus voltage
  • Minimum and maximum bus voltage
  • Continuous current limit
  • Peak current limit and duration
  • Battery or power-supply capability
  • Regenerative-energy handling
  • Emergency-stop behavior
  • Cable and connector current capacity

The controller current limit directly affects available torque. Electrical limits must be checked together with the motor, thermal design and duty cycle.

docs.title: Step 11: Evaluate Thermal Conditions and Duty Cycle
docs.text:
Provide:

  • Ambient temperature
  • Operating time
  • Holding time
  • Rest time
  • Cycle frequency
  • Enclosure and mounting material
  • Cooling method
  • Airflow or conduction path
  • Nearby heat sources

A joint mounted inside a sealed limb or compact housing may behave differently from the same actuator tested in open air. Prototype testing should reproduce the planned installation and motion cycle.

docs.title: Step 12: Define Brake, Safety and Power-Off Behavior
docs.text:
For gravity-loaded, wearable or safety-related axes, specify:

  • Whether the joint may move when power is removed
  • Required holding torque
  • Mechanical brake requirement
  • Emergency-stop behavior
  • Manual release requirement
  • Safe direction of motion
  • Collision or overload strategy

A brake must not be assumed to be included unless it is explicitly confirmed in the selected configuration and quotation.

docs.title: Step 13: Plan Prototype Validation
docs.text:
Prototype testing should include representative:

  • Payload and link geometry
  • Continuous motion cycles
  • Peak events
  • Temperature monitoring
  • Holding conditions
  • Direction reversals
  • Encoder behavior
  • Controller current limits
  • Communication behavior
  • External loads
  • Power-off and emergency-stop cases

Selection is complete only after the actuator is validated in the actual or representative mechanism.

docs.text:
